outline: Embryonic development, fetal maturation, and perinatal transitional changes
Congenital disorders involving chambers and valves
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Failure of normal delamination of the septal and posterior tricuspid valve leaflets from the right ventricular myocardium causes apical displacement of the valve. The proximal portion of the right ventricle becomes functionally incorporated into the right atrium ('atrialized'), promoting tricuspid regurgitation, right atrial enlargement, and a high prevalence of accessory atrioventricular pathways.
vignette: A 16-year-old boy is evaluated for episodic palpitations and mild exertional cyanosis. Cardiac examination shows a holosystolic murmur that increases with inspiration. ECG during sinus rhythm shows a short PR interval and a delta wave. Echocardiography shows severe tricuspid regurgitation, marked right atrial enlargement, and a tricuspid valve whose septal leaflet inserts abnormally far toward the right ventricular apex. A portion of the proximal right ventricle functions as part of the right atrium.
lead: Which developmental abnormality most directly produced this patient’s cardiac malformation?
correct: Failure of normal delamination of tricuspid valve leaflets from the right ventricular myocardium
distractors: Abnormal neural crest migration causing defective separation of the aorta and pulmonary trunk
Failure of endocardial cushion fusion causing a common atrioventricular junction
Excessive resorption of the septum primum with inadequate development of the septum secundum
Failure of postnatal closure of the ductus arteriosus
distractor_notes: Abnormal neural crest migration causes conotruncal defects such as persistent truncus arteriosus and contributes to tetralogy of Fallot, not apical displacement of the tricuspid valve.

Failure of endocardial cushion fusion causes atrioventricular septal defects with abnormalities of the AV septum and common/abnormal AV valves, not atrialization of the right ventricle from a displaced tricuspid valve.
Excessive septum-primum resorption or inadequate septum-secundum development can produce a secundum atrial septal defect but does not cause tricuspid-leaflet displacement.
Persistent ductus arteriosus is failure of postnatal ductal closure and creates an aortopulmonary shunt rather than a displaced tricuspid valve.
key_expl: The echocardiographic finding of apical displacement of the septal tricuspid leaflet with an 'atrialized' proximal right ventricle is diagnostic of Ebstein anomaly. The developmental lesion is failure of normal delamination of the tricuspid valve leaflets—especially the septal and posterior leaflets—from the right ventricular myocardium. Poor leaflet coaptation causes tricuspid regurgitation and marked right atrial enlargement. Accessory atrioventricular pathways are common, explaining the ventricular preexcitation pattern in this patient.
objective: Explain Ebstein anomaly as failed delamination and apical displacement of the tricuspid valve, producing atrialization of the proximal right ventricle, tricuspid regurgitation, and susceptibility to accessory-pathway tachyarrhythmias.
clues: short PR interval and delta wave
